topic: How Color Works: a 90-minute hands-on workshop

facts.claim: NASA Science states the human eye typically detects wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometers, with violet at the short end (~380 nm) and red at the long end (~700 nm).
facts.source_title: Visible Light - NASA Science

facts.claim: Compiled physics references show the cited visible-spectrum range varies by source (commonly 380-700 nm, but also stated as 380-750 nm, 400-700 nm, or 380-780 nm depending on the textbook), indicating the spectrum's edges are a conventional, gradually-fading boundary rather than a sharp physical cutoff.
facts.source_title: Wavelength Range of Visible Light - The Physics Factbook

facts.claim: Human color vision is trichromatic: the retina has three classes of cone photoreceptor, conventionally labeled S (short-wavelength), M (medium-wavelength), and L (long-wavelength), each named for the region of the visible spectrum where its sensitivity peaks.
facts.source_title: Visual pigments of rods and cones in a human retina

facts.claim: Bowmaker & Dartnall's 1980 microspectrophotometry of human retinal outer segments (Journal of Physiology, vol. 298) measured mean photopigment absorbance peaks at approximately 420 nm for S ("blue") cones, 534 nm for M ("green") cones, and 563 nm for L ("red") cones.
facts.source_title: Bowmaker JK & Dartnall HJ (1980), Visual pigments of rods and cones in a human retina, J Physiol 298:501-511

facts.claim: The human retina contains approximately 6 million cone photoreceptors, compared with roughly 120 million rods; cones make up only about 5% of total photoreceptors but are concentrated in the fovea, where they support fine detail and color vision.
facts.source_title: Neuroanatomy, Retina - StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

facts.claim: The Colour & Vision Research Laboratory (CVRL) database, hosted at the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology, publishes the Stockman & Sharpe (2000) 2-degree cone fundamentals as downloadable tables at 0.1, 1, and 5 nm wavelength steps; these functions have been adopted by the CIE as its physiologically-relevant standard colorimetric functions. Exact numeric (wavelength, S, M, L) rows could not be retrieved through the tools available to this research pass, so a full plotted table is not sourced here -- only the dataset's existence, provenance, and CIE adoption are confirmed.
facts.source_title: Colour & Vision Research Laboratory (CVRL) - Stockman and Sharpe (2000) 2-deg cone fundamentals

facts.claim: Additive color mixing combines colored light: it starts from black (absence of light) and adds red, green, and blue light, with red+green+blue at full intensity producing white; this is the model behind all screen-based media (monitors, phones, projectors).
facts.source_title: Additive and subtractive colour systems - Colour Theory: Understanding and Working with Colour (RMIT)

facts.claim: Subtractive color mixing combines physical pigments, inks, or dyes: it starts from white (fully reflected light) and each added cyan, magenta, or yellow pigment absorbs (subtracts) certain wavelengths, so mixing more pigment makes the result darker; this is the model behind all physical print (commercial printing, inkjet, laser).
facts.source_title: Additive and subtractive colour systems - Colour Theory: Understanding and Working with Colour (RMIT)

facts.claim: The additive primaries (red, green, blue) and the subtractive primaries (cyan, magenta, yellow) are complements of each other: each additive primary is the secondary mixture of the subtractive system, and vice versa.
facts.source_title: Additive and subtractive colour systems - Colour Theory: Understanding and Working with Colour (RMIT)

facts.claim: The HSL color model, defined in the W3C CSS Color specification, represents a color as hue (an angle on a 0-360 degree color circle, with red at 0/360, green at 120, blue at 240), saturation (a percentage, 100% fully saturated, 0% gray), and lightness (a percentage, 0% black, 100% white, 50% a color's 'normal' tone).
facts.source_title: CSS Color Module Level 4 (W3C)

facts.claim: WCAG's text contrast requirement (Success Criterion 1.4.3) is defined purely as a function of the two colors' relative luminance -- not their hue or saturation -- so under the W3C's own accessibility model, legibility contrast is fundamentally a lightness/luminance property rather than a hue-difference or saturation-difference property.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG defines relative luminance for the sRGB color space as L = 0.2126*R + 0.7152*G + 0.0722*B, where R, G, and B are gamma-linearized channel values (each channel divided by 12.92 if its sRGB value is <= 0.04045, otherwise raised through the ((value+0.055)/1.055)^2.4 transform).
facts.source_title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 - Relative luminance definition

facts.claim: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum, Level AA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between normal text and its background.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum, Level AA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between large-scale text and its background.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG defines 'large text' as at least 18 point, or at least 14 point and bold, or a font size that yields an equivalent visual size for CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) fonts; the specification's own conversion notes 14pt and 18pt as approximately 18.5px and 24px.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.6 (Contrast Enhanced, Level AAA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 7:1 between normal text (below 18pt regular / 14pt bold) and its background.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.6: Contrast (Enhanced) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.6 (Contrast Enhanced, Level AAA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for large text (18pt+ regular or 14pt+ bold).
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.6: Contrast (Enhanced) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast, Level AA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 3:1, against adjacent colors, for the visual presentation of user interface components and of graphical objects required to understand the content.
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast - W3C WAI

facts.claim: WCAG's contrast ratio is computed as (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 and L2 are the relative luminances of the lighter and darker of the two colors; the resulting ratio ranges from 1:1 to 21:1 and must not be rounded when checked against a threshold (e.g. a computed 4.499:1 does not meet a 4.5:1 requirement).
facts.source_title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: The U.S. National Eye Institute states that about 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency, and that men have a much higher risk than women.
facts.source_title: Color Blindness - National Eye Institute (NIH)

facts.claim: Worldwide, an estimated 8% of men and 0.5% of women have a red-green type of color vision deficiency (roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women), with reported rates rising to about 10-11% of men in some Scandinavian/Northern European populations.
facts.source_title: Types of Colour Blindness - Colour Blind Awareness

facts.claim: Within the approximately 8% of men with inherited red-green color vision deficiency, the split by type is roughly: 5% deuteranomalous (the single most common type), 1% deuteranopes, 1% protanomalous, and 1% protanopes.
facts.source_title: Types of Colour Blindness - Colour Blind Awareness

facts.claim: Blue-yellow color vision deficiency (tritanopia/tritanomaly) and total color blindness (achromatopsia) are both much rarer than red-green deficiency, affecting on the order of 1 in 30,000 to 1 in 50,000 people.
facts.source_title: Types of Colour Blindness - Colour Blind Awareness

facts.claim: Johannes Itten's twelve-hue color wheel, published in his 1961 book 'The Art of Color' and rooted in the color course he taught at the Bauhaus school in the 1920s, is the commonly-taught basis for schemes such as complementary, analogous, and triadic color pairing; Itten treated these as one of seven categories of color contrast he catalogued for design teaching, not as a physical law.
facts.source_title: Color | Bauhaus - The Getty Research Institute

facts.claim: Albert Munsell's color system, an alternative to Itten's wheel, was built to divide hues into perceptually equal steps; because different color models and color spaces yield different pairs of 'complementary' or 'harmonious' hues, the specific schemes taught in design (complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary) are conventions of a chosen model rather than a single physical fact about light or pigment.
facts.source_title: Harmony (color) - Wikipedia

facts.claim: Because humans can perceptually distinguish on the order of millions of distinct colors, researchers (Hard & Sivik, 2001, cited via the Wikipedia 'Harmony (color)' overview) have argued that fixed predictive color-harmony formulae are fundamentally unsound as universal rules, since harmony judgments depend on context, perception, and the specific color model chosen.
facts.source_title: Harmony (color) - Wikipedia (citing Hard & Sivik, 2001)

facts.claim: Borland & Taylor's 2007 paper 'Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful' (IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, vol. 27, issue 2, pp. 14-17) argues the rainbow color map is rarely the optimal choice for visualizing ordered data because it lacks perceptual ordering (equal-looking steps do not correspond to equal data steps), obscures data through uncontrolled luminance variation across hues, and can actively mislead interpretation through gradients unrelated to the underlying data.
facts.source_title: Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful

facts.claim: Crameri, Shephard & Heron's 2020 paper 'The misuse of colour in science communication' (Nature Communications, vol. 11, article 5444) documents that rainbow-like and red-green color maps remain common in published science despite visually distorting data through uneven color gradients and being unreadable to people with color-vision deficiency, and it proposes perceptually uniform 'scientific colour maps' as a fix.
facts.source_title: The misuse of colour in science communication - Nature Communications

facts.claim: Katsushika Hokusai's 'Under the Wave off Kanagawa' (also known as 'The Great Wave'), from the series 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji,' is a polychrome woodblock print made circa 1830-32 during Japan's Edo period, and is held in the collection of The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
facts.source_title: Katsushika Hokusai - Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave) - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

facts.claim: The Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access program, launched February 7, 2017, releases images and data for artworks the Museum believes to be in the public domain -- including 'The Great Wave' -- under a Creative Commons Zero (CC0) designation, for unrestricted commercial and noncommercial reuse without permission or fee.
facts.source_title: Open Access - The Metropolitan Museum of Art

facts.claim: WebAIM's Contrast Checker is a free web tool that computes the WCAG contrast ratio between two colors and reports whether it passes the AA/AAA thresholds for normal and large text.
facts.source_title: WebAIM: Contrast Checker

facts.claim: The W3C's 'How to Meet WCAG (Quick Reference)' is a filterable reference listing every WCAG success criterion and technique, filterable by conformance level (A/AA/AAA), technology, and topic.
facts.source_title: How to Meet WCAG (Quick Reference) - W3C WAI

facts.claim: Coblis (Color Blindness Simulator) is a free web tool that lets a user upload an image and view a simulated rendering of how it would appear to someone with each major type of color vision deficiency.
facts.source_title: Coblis - Color Blindness Simulator (Colblindor)

facts.claim: ColorBrewer is a free tool for choosing sequential, diverging, and qualitative color schemes intended for maps and other data visualizations.
facts.source_title: ColorBrewer: Color Advice for Maps

facts.claim: Adobe Color is a free web app for building, exploring, and extracting color themes, including rule-based harmony generators (complementary, analogous, triadic, and others).
facts.source_title: Adobe Color

facts.claim: The Colour & Vision Research Laboratory (CVRL) database, maintained at the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology, is a public library of downloadable standard color-and-vision datasets, including the Stockman & Sharpe (2000) cone fundamentals and CIE colorimetric functions.
facts.source_title: CVRL - Colour & Vision Research Laboratory
